school: Development Economics, Welfare Economics, International Economics
legacy: Ian Little helped shape modern development economics by emphasizing practical analysis, clear reasoning, and evidence-based public policy. His work encouraged economists to evaluate development programs according to their real impact on human well-being rather than abstract theoretical goals alone. Through research and teaching, he influenced how governments, international organizations, and scholars think about economic growth, resource allocation, and poverty reduction.
earlyLife: Little developed an early interest in public affairs, economics, and social improvement. His education exposed him to questions concerning economic organization, international trade, and the challenges facing developing societies. These experiences fostered a lifelong interest in understanding how economic policies affect living standards and opportunities for growth.
scientificField: Economics, Development Economics, Welfare Economics, Public Policy
majorContributions: Little contributed to economic thought through research on development strategies, welfare analysis, and project evaluation. He argued that economic policies should be assessed according to measurable outcomes and their effects on people's lives. His work helped refine methods for comparing policy alternatives and evaluating large public investments. He also explored the role of international trade, economic incentives, and institutional effectiveness in promoting long-term development and prosperity.
laterLife: Throughout his later career, Little continued writing, teaching, and advising on issues related to development and public policy. He participated in debates concerning economic planning, poverty reduction, and international development. His later works emphasized the importance of practical judgment, empirical evidence, and careful policy design when addressing complex economic problems.
whyImportant: Ian Little is important because he helped make development economics more analytical and policy-oriented. His research encouraged economists and decision-makers to focus on outcomes, efficiency, and human welfare when evaluating economic programs. Many modern approaches to project assessment and development policy reflect principles that he helped advance.
